claims.text: A model combining machine-learned interatomic potentials with coupled Boltzmann transport calculations can separately predict lattice and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Interatomic-potential modeling can capture relevant atomistic complexity in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed model will accurately account for realistic defects and 1 wt.% oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr.
The applicable material is bulk crystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing defects and 1 wt.% oxygen.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are nearly comparable.
A HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen has total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) from 300 to 1200 K.
Oxygen impurities affect the high-temperature thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect distributions and oxygen-induced local lattice distortions mediate phonon and electron conduction in HfNbTaTiZr.

Separately representing anharmonic phonon scattering and electron-phonon coupling, rather than using one Debye temperature or a perfect-crystal approximation, will yield independent lattice and electronic conductivity predictions.
Existing analytical approaches and simulations either conflate lattice and electronic transport or rely on Debye-temperature models and perfect, defect-free crystals.
The model will predict nearly equal lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K.
From 300 to 1200 K, the predicted total conductivity will match measurements in the range 10–17 W/(K m).
The proposed model will reduce overall prediction error by approximately 20% relative to earlier analytical models.
The model is applicable to well-characterized bulk HfNbTaTiZr with controlled oxygen content from below 200 K to about 1200 K.
Predictions will become less reliable outside the stated temperature range or when the actual defect distribution differs strongly from the modeled distribution.
Electrical conductivity combined with the Wiedemann–Franz law can be used to estimate the electronic contribution independently from the lattice contribution.
Failure to observe nearly equal contributions below 200 K, total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m) at 300–1200 K, or an approximately 20% error reduction would falsify the hypothesis.
